senses: a parent’s tender love for a child
kind, loving (of the stronger toward the weaker)
慈石: the “loving stone”, a magnet
慈.shuowenEn: To love. From 心 (heart), with 兹 for the sound.

parts.m: plants that grow more and more; also the sound

慈.story: 慈 is the love that runs downward: parent to child, and first of all the mother’s. Its partner is 孝, the child’s devotion upward. The Laozi names the pair in passages 18 and 19, where 孝慈 appear only after the family has lost its ease, and return when clever virtue is given up. In passage 67 慈 is the first of three precious things and the root of courage; heaven guards with it those it would save. The Mawangdui silk texts write it 茲, with no heart. Early texts call the magnet 慈石, the loving stone that draws iron as a mother draws her child.
慈.gap: “Compassion” is a later Buddhist colour; “mercy” needs a judge; “gentleness” is a manner. 慈 is a force: it feeds, carries, and defends, and it flows from strength toward what is small.

儉.shuowenEn: To bind, to restrain. From 人 (person), with 僉 for the sound.
儉.story: 儉 is the conduct of a person who holds in: few wants, little display, small cost to others. Confucians praised it in ritual and in a ruler’s household. The Laozi uses the word only in passage 67, as the second of three precious things: 儉故能廣, sparing and so able to be wide. Wang Bi explains that when cost is spared the world does not run short. Passage 59 praises a related quality with another word, 嗇, the farmer’s care in storing. The opposite is 奢, lavish, “stretched open”. The Mawangdui silk texts write the word with the graph 檢.
儉.gap: “Economy” is bookkeeping, “moderation” is a mean between extremes, “frugality” is about money. 儉 is a general drawing-in of the self, so that there is more room around it.

senses: in front, ahead; to go first
forebears, the dead of earlier generations
先.shuowenEn: To go forward. From 儿 (a person) and 之 (to go).

parts.m: to go; a foot setting out (upper part, reshaped)

先.story: The early graph is commonly explained as a foot above a person: the one whose foot has gone ahead. It means first in place and first in time, and so the ancestors. The Laozi is wary of the front. The sage puts the body behind and the body comes first (7). To be ahead of the people one must put the body behind them (66). The third treasure is 不敢為天下先, not daring to go ahead of the world (67). The Dao itself is the one exception: it seems to be earlier than the Lord on high (4) and was born before heaven and earth (25).
先.gap: English separates “first” (rank), “before” (time), and “ancestor”. 先 is all three, so “not to be the world’s 先” refuses rank, priority, and fatherhood at once.

senses: to resemble, to be like (as kin are alike)
不肖: unlike one’s forebears; unworthy, good for nothing
肖.shuowen: 骨肉相似也。从肉小聲。不似其先，故曰“不肖”也。
肖.shuowenEn: Bone and flesh that are alike. From 肉 (flesh), with 小 for the sound. One who is not like his forebears is therefore called 不肖.
肖.story: 肖 is family likeness: the child’s face that repeats the parent’s. 不肖, “not like”, was the common word for a son who fell short of his father, and then for any worthless person; it is the opposite of 賢, worthy. Passage 67 plays on both senses. The world says the speaker’s Dao is great and 不肖: like nothing, and so no good. The speaker answers that only the great is unlike; a thing that resembled another would long ago have been small. The sound part of the graph is 小, small. The modern word for a portrait is 肖像.
肖.gap: “Unlike” loses the insult and “unworthy” loses the likeness. The pun needs a family: a child of whom people say, “who does it take after?”

senses: (of a ruler) the seal; things of the throne
寶.shuowen: 珍也。从宀从王从貝，缶聲。
寶.shuowenEn: A precious thing. From 宀 (roof), 王 (here: jade), and 貝 (cowrie shell), with 缶 (jar) for the sound.
寶.story: Jade and shell money under a roof: what a house stores and guards. The Laozi takes the word of wealth and gives it other contents. The Dao is the treasure of the good person (62). The speaker has three precious things: tenderness, spareness, and not daring to go ahead of the world (67). To take the enemy lightly is nearly to lose “my treasures” (69). The sage wears coarse cloth and holds jade in the bosom (70). The word is a homophone of 保, to keep safe, and passage 67 joins them: 持而保之. Buddhists later used 三寶 for their Three Jewels.
寶.gap: “Treasure” in English is gold in a chest. The Laozi’s 寶 are not objects at all; the word is used against its own picture.

勇.shuowenEn: It is breath, vital energy. From 力 (strength), with 甬 for the sound.
勇.story: The Shuowen defines courage as 气, breath: the surge of energy that carries a body forward. It was the prized quality of the Warring States, rewarded with rank and sung in stories of swordsmen. The Laozi gives it conditions. Courage grows from tenderness, and courage with the tenderness let go is death (67). Courage in daring kills; courage in not-daring keeps alive (73). Confucius drew a similar line: the humane are sure to be brave, and the brave are not sure to be humane.
勇.gap: “Brave” is praise in English with no question asked. 勇 is a raw force of breath and strength; the texts ask what it serves.

senses: to guard, to stand guard around
a guard, an escort; the night watch
Wei: a state of the central plain
衛.shuowen: 宿衞也。从韋、帀，从行。行，列衞也。
衛.shuowenEn: The night guard. From 韋 and 帀 (to go round), and from 行; 行 is the ranks of the guards. (The Shuowen writes the graph 衞.)

parts.m: commonly explained as feet circling a walled place

衛.story: 衛 is a patrol: guards who walk around a place at night. It named a ruler’s bodyguard and the border posts of a state, and it is the name of an old state near the Yellow River. In the Laozi it comes once, in the last line of passage 67: 天將救之，以慈衛之, heaven will rescue them and guard them with tenderness. The Mawangdui silk texts have “wall them round” in its place. Later medicine took the word for the body’s defensive energy, 衛氣, which circles at the surface.
衛.gap: “Protect” is general. 衛 is a ring of sentries in motion, a military picture used for a mother’s care.

senses: to hold on to, to maintain
保.shuowenEn: To nurture. From 人 (person) and a reduced 𤓽; 𤓽 is the ancient form of 孚.

parts.m: commonly explained as a child carried on the back (shape reshaped)

保.story: The early form is commonly explained as a person with a child on the back, and the Shuowen defines the word as “to nurture”. From child care came the wider sense “to keep safe”. In the Laozi it is the verb for things that are easily lost. One who keeps (保) this Dao does not wish to be full (15). A hall full of gold and jade cannot be kept (9). The three precious things are held and kept (67). The Dao is what the not-good person is kept by (62). The word is a homophone of 寶, treasure.
保.gap: “Preserve” and “protect” are cool words. 保 has a carried child in it: to keep is to bear on one’s own back.
